title: Fragmentation
summary: Internal vs external fragmentation, why external fragmentation gets worse the longer a system runs, and why paging kills one but not the other.

slides.markdown:
"Fragmentation" is memory that's technically free but effectively unusable — and it comes in two flavors that get confused constantly in interviews. **Internal fragmentation** is waste *inside* a block you were given. **External fragmentation** is waste *between* blocks, scattered across many small unusable gaps.

The distinction matters because the fixes are completely different: internal fragmentation is solved by allocating in smaller units; external fragmentation is solved by either compacting memory or, more practically, never requiring contiguous physical placement in the first place — which is exactly what paging does.

slides.sectionTitle: Internal fragmentation: wasted space inside an allocated block
slides.markdown:
**Internal fragmentation** happens when a process is given more memory than it asked for, because the allocator only hands out memory in fixed-size units. If pages are 4 KB and a process needs 4097 bytes, it gets two full pages (8 KB) — the last 4095 bytes of the second page are allocated to this process and unusable by anyone else, forever, until the process frees that page.

The defining trait: this waste is invisible to the free-list bookkeeping — the OS correctly reports that block as "fully allocated," it's just that the process using it doesn't need all of it. On average, a system using N-byte allocation units wastes about N/2 bytes per allocation to internal fragmentation.

slides.sectionTitle: External fragmentation: wasted space between allocated blocks
slides.markdown:
**External fragmentation** happens when there's enough *total* free memory to satisfy a request, but no single free block is big enough, because the free space is scattered in pieces between allocated blocks. A system might have 500 MB free split across fifty 10 MB holes, and still be unable to satisfy a single 50 MB request.

Unlike internal fragmentation, this waste is visible in the free-list total — the bookkeeping correctly says "500 MB free" — but that number is misleading about what's actually usable. External fragmentation is a direct consequence of contiguous, variable-size allocation: as processes of different sizes come and go, the holes they leave behind are different sizes too, and rarely line up with the next request.

The visual tell: internal fragmentation is waste trapped *inside* one process's own block; external fragmentation is waste trapped *between* different processes' blocks.

slides.sectionTitle: Why external fragmentation gets worse over time: the 50% rule
slides.markdown:
External fragmentation isn't a one-time cost — it compounds. Every time a block is allocated and later freed, the freed hole's size depends on what happened to be requested and released, not on any plan. Over many allocate/free cycles, holes keep splitting into oddly-sized pieces that rarely exactly match the next request.

Knuth's **50% rule** (also called the "half rule," derived from analysis and confirmed by simulation) says that under first-fit allocation, for every N blocks currently allocated, roughly N/2 additional unusable holes tend to form. In other words, fragmentation grows roughly in proportion to the *number* of allocations that have happened, not just how full memory is — a long-running system with heavy allocate/free churn fragments even if average utilization stays moderate.

**Compaction** fixes external fragmentation directly: the OS shifts allocated blocks so all the free space merges into one large contiguous region, the same way disk defragmentation consolidates scattered files.

It only works if binding is execution-time (base/limit registers or a translation layer you can just update after the move) — compaction is impossible for compile-time or load-time bound programs, since their addresses can't change once fixed. Even where it's possible, compaction is expensive: every relocated process has to be paused while its (potentially large) memory image is copied, so real systems avoid running it often, and general-purpose OSes today mostly avoid needing it at all by using paging instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Why paging was invented partly to kill external fragmentation
slides.markdown:
External fragmentation exists specifically because contiguous allocation demands a single unbroken physical range per process. **Paging** removes that constraint at the root: a process's pages can live in *any* physical frames, scattered arbitrarily, because the page table records the mapping for each page independently.

That means the only requirement for satisfying an allocation is having *enough free frames total*, not one contiguous run of them — external fragmentation, as a concept, simply doesn't apply to page frames. This is one of paging's two founding motivations (the other being flexible, execution-time relocation for swapping); see [Paging Fundamentals](paging-fundamentals) for how the page table makes this work.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: fixed-size vs variable-size allocation — which fragmentation type each trades for
slides.markdown:
| | Fixed-size units (e.g. paging, fixed partitions) | Variable-size units (e.g. segmentation, contiguous allocation) |
|---|---|---|
| Internal fragmentation | Yes — last partial unit is wasted | No — allocated exactly to size |
| External fragmentation | No — any free unit fits any request needing one unit | Yes — free space splinters into odd-sized, hard-to-reuse holes |
| Worst case per allocation | Bounded: at most (unit size − 1) bytes wasted | Unbounded: an allocation can fail despite ample total free memory |
| Typical fix | Use a smaller unit size to shrink the waste | Compaction, or switch to fixed-size units entirely |

The pattern worth remembering: you don't eliminate fragmentation, you choose *which kind* you're willing to live with. Real systems (page-based virtual memory) pick internal fragmentation deliberately, because it's bounded and predictable — external fragmentation isn't.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reporting free memory without checking usable block sizes
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The system reports 2 GB free, so a 1 GB allocation should always succeed."

**Why it's wrong:** under contiguous, variable-size allocation, "free" is a sum across every hole, however small — 2 GB free could be four thousand 500 KB holes, none anywhere close to 1 GB. The allocation fails not because memory ran out, but because it's fragmented past the point of usefulness.

**Correct model:** always ask "free in what unit, and how contiguous does it need to be?" This is precisely why page-based systems report memory in terms of free *frames* rather than free *bytes* for allocation purposes — a frame is always immediately usable on its own, so the number means what it says.

slides.sectionTitle: The nuance interviewers probe for: fragmentation didn't disappear, it moved
slides.markdown:
A common staff-level follow-up: "if paging solved fragmentation, why do modern systems still talk about it?" The honest answer is that paging solved *external* fragmentation for physical memory, but the problem resurfaces in adjacent places. Kernel allocators that need physically contiguous multi-page regions (for DMA buffers, huge pages, or certain driver requirements) can still suffer external fragmentation across page *frames* — this is exactly why Linux's buddy allocator exists, to keep larger contiguous runs of frames available.

Similarly, `malloc`'s heap inside a process is built on variable-size chunks and gets external fragmentation of its own, independent of the OS's paging underneath it. "We solved fragmentation" is never quite true — it's solved at one layer and reappears, in a smaller and more contained form, at the next.
